absent: Locking discipline for shrinker registration, cache creation, allocation, free and sheaf exchange is not shown.
Internal layout of shrinker, kmem_cache, sheaf, barn, bucket and large allocation descriptors beyond referenced fields is not shown.
Implementation of cache creation, destruction, bulk transfer, node placement, large allocation, reclaim and debug helpers is not shown.
Error handling beyond default argument rejection and out of range size fatal handling is not shown.
Concurrency, sleeping, interrupt and preemption constraints for allocation entry points are not shown.
Configuration meanings for partition modes, tiny caches and sanitizer interactions beyond flag collapsing are not shown.

findings.text: Reclaim capability selection uses three distinct low bit positions, one marking node aware scanning, one marking memory group aware scanning, and one marking non slab objects.

Reference acquisition succeeds only while the target remains alive and leaves state unchanged on failure, while release drops one reference and signals completion exactly when the last reference disappears.
A debug filesystem rename helper is exposed that accepts a target plus formatted name arguments and reports success unconditionally in the shown configuration.
A conventional include guard macro marks the slab header as included.

Slab cache options are single bit flags derived from a private enumeration of bit positions covering debugging, poisoning, alignment, placement, tracking, panic, type safety, tracing, merging, accounting, sanitizers, reclaim, extensions and sheaf behaviour.

Several slab options collapse to a zero value when supporting features are disabled and select their dedicated bit when enabled, covering debug objects, failure injection, memory group accounting variants, sanitizer handling, fence skipping, reclaim accounting and object extension placement.
A temporary object marker is defined as an alias of the reclaim accounting flag and denotes short lived contents.

Cache creation parameters are grouped in one record holding alignment, user copy offset and length, custom free pointer offset with a validity marker, a construction callback, and a sheaf capacity, where zero or null values select defaults meaning no special alignment, no user window, no callback and no sheaves.

Custom free pointer placement is allowed only for type safe or constructor equipped caches, zero is a usable offset when explicitly enabled, and callers must avoid overlaying fields that guard against recycling or that the constructor initializes.

Sheaf caching maintains per processor main and spare object stores backed by per node reserves, exchanging empty stores for full ones on allocation and full stores for empty ones on release, refilling or draining through bulk slab operations when exchange is unavailable or reserves overflow, falling back to direct slab use when blocking is forbidden, bypassing for explicit node requests, and disabling entirely under slab debugging.

Cache creation is available through a basic form with alignment and constructor, a user copy form with window plus constructor, and a default form that rejects any caller supplied parameter block, alongside helpers that derive name size and natural alignment from a structure type and optionally derive a user window from a named member.

Allocation site tokens appear in two shapes selected by configuration, one holding an unsigned value and one empty, with creation helpers that either capture location or inference data, capture a constant zero, or produce a neutral token.

Declaration and forwarding helpers for token and bucket augmented size parameters either expand to extra arguments or to nothing, allowing shared call sites to compile with or without tracking and bucket selection.
Zero length allocation yields a small fixed nonzero sentinel distinct from null, and a predicate treats any address at or below that sentinel as null like.

General allocation geometry defines an architecture minimum size and alignment, shift bounds derived from page size and maximum page order, separate ceilings for cache backed and total sizes, a maximum order, and a minimum slab object size clamped upward for very small minima.

Size class caches are partitioned by usage kind including normal, reclaimable, direct memory access, group charged, extension free and optional partitions, with several kinds aliasing to normal when their feature is off, and buckets form a table sized by the high shift.

Cache kind selection stays on the normal path for common flag combinations and otherwise applies fixed priority with direct access first, then reclaimable, then group charged, while normal requests may spread across partition copies by hash or by token value.

Size to index mapping sends zero to zero, tiny sizes to the low shift, offers two packed intermediate buckets for economy, then follows doubling steps from single bytes up to two megabytes, treating larger sizes as a fatal programming error with a stronger diagnostic for constant sizes.

Allocation is exposed through cache paths for generic, least recently used, bulk, node specific and sheaf specific use, byte paths for blocking and non blocking contexts, resizing helpers defaulting to unit alignment and no node preference, and a raw bulk free that routes through cache bulk release with a null cache.

Constant sized byte requests above the cache ceiling use a large object path, other constant sizes use an indexed cache chosen by size and flags, and dynamically sized requests use a generic byte path.

Type aware helpers compute single object, counted array and flexible array sizes from a type and count, allocate through zeroing, non zeroing or virtual capable paths with default flags, and record the requested count in the trailing flexible member on success.

An object description helper reports absence in the shown configuration, an alignment query returns the architecture slab minimum, and assumption markers advertise kmalloc, slab and page alignment guarantees.
Supplying a parameter block to the default argument creator triggers a one time warning and produces an error pointer, and requesting an index for an out of range size is fatal.
Incorrect custom free pointer placement can corrupt recycling protection or constructor state, and sheaf allocation does not preserve node placement.
